common_name: TAM Mild Jalapeno Pepper (Low-Heat Texas A&M Jalapeno)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; TAM Mild was bred at Texas A&M to keep the classic jalapeno shape and flavor while cutting the heat to a fraction of a standard jalapeno's, making it a good choice for gardeners who want jalapeno flavor without much bite.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date, and harvest fruit at any stage from glossy dark green through fully ripe red. TAM Mild Jalapeno was developed by the Texas A&M AgriLife breeding program specifically to lower the capsaicin content of a standard jalapeno to a mild 500-2,500 Scoville units, roughly a tenth the heat of a typical jalapeno, while keeping the same thick-walled, classic jalapeno shape, size, and flavor that makes it useful for salsas, poppers, and pickling. The compact, productive plants set fruit heavily over a long season and tolerate Southern heat well, though heat and moisture stress can occasionally nudge individual peppers hotter than the variety's baseline. It's a good choice for gardeners, and especially families with children, who want the jalapeno's flavor and crunch without much of its punch.

common_name: Urfa Biber Pepper (Turkish Sun-Dried Smoky Raisin Pepper)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Urfa Biber is grown primarily as a drying and spice pepper, traditionally harvested fully ripe, sun-dried by day and sweated under cover by night, a slow process that gives the finished flakes their deep purple-black color and raisiny, smoky flavor.

directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger passes, then let fruit ripen fully to deep red before harvesting for drying. Urfa Biber takes its name from the city of Sanliurfa in southeastern Turkey, where the pepper is traditionally processed by day-drying the ripe fruit in the sun and wrapping or covering it at night so it sweats and partially reabsorbs moisture, a cycle repeated over several days that develops its signature near-black color, raisin-like sweetness, and mild, smoky, wine-like heat around 30,000-50,000 Scoville units. The moist, oily flakes it produces are a staple spice in Turkish and increasingly in Western kitchens, used to finish roasted vegetables, meats, and eggs where a coarser, sweeter, less sharply hot flavor than crushed red pepper is wanted. A single well-grown plant can produce enough fruit for a good supply of home-dried flakes, and the peppers can also be strung and air-dried in a covered, well-ventilated spot if a controlled sweating setup isn't practical.

common_name: Amish Pie Pumpkin (Heirloom Sweet Baking Pumpkin)

planting.note: Direct sow into warm soil after frost danger has passed; Amish Pie is a Plain-community heirloom pumpkin grown for its dense, sweet, fine-grained flesh, prized above the watery flesh of jack-o'-lantern types for baking.

directions: Sow seed an inch deep in hills of warm, fertile soil and give the sprawling vines plenty of room to run, or trellis smaller fruit for a large vertical crop. Amish Pie is a heritage pumpkin passed down through Plain communities for its large, ribbed, deep-orange fruit and thick, dense, notably sweet flesh, considered by many bakers superior to jack-o'-lantern pumpkins, which tend to be stringy and watery by comparison. Fruits commonly run 10-20 pounds and store well into winter in a cool, dry spot, making it practical to bake from a single pumpkin over several months. Keep vines well watered as fruit sizes up and reduce watering as the rind hardens and colors fully in fall, then cure harvested pumpkins for a week or two before storage to concentrate sweetness and toughen the skin.

common_name: Speckled Hound Pumpkin (Green-Speckled Orange Heirloom Baking Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow into warm soil after frost danger has passed; Speckled Hound is a moschata-type heirloom pumpkin with distinctive dark green speckling over an orange rind and dense, sweet, moist flesh good for pies and roasting.

directions: Sow seed an inch deep in hills of warm, fertile soil and give the vigorous vines room to sprawl, since Speckled Hound belongs to Cucurbita moschata, the same heat- and pest-tolerant species as butternut squash and generally outperforms Cucurbita pepo pumpkins in hot, humid Southern gardens. The medium-sized, slightly flattened fruit has a striking dark green speckled pattern over deep orange skin, and the moist, dense, sweet flesh is well suited to pies, soups, and roasting, holding its flavor and texture through long storage better than most jack-o'-lantern types. Moschata squash also tends to shrug off vine borers better than pepo types, a real advantage in the Gulf South where borers are a persistent problem. Harvest once the rind resists a fingernail scratch and the stem has begun to dry, and cure fruit in a warm, airy spot for a week or two before moving to cool winter storage.

common_name: Georgia Streak Tomato (Southern Heirloom Bicolor Beefsteak)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Georgia Streak is a Southern heirloom bicolor beefsteak with a yellow background marbled in red, grown for its sweet, low-acid flavor and striking sliced appearance.

directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date and stake or cage the vigorous indeterminate vines early. Georgia Streak is a Southern heirloom beefsteak in the same bicolor family as Pineapple and Hillbilly, producing large, golden-yellow fruit marbled and streaked with red through the flesh as well as the skin, so each slice shows the same vivid marbling as the exterior. The flavor is sweet and mild with low acidity, characteristic of yellow-red bicolor heirlooms, and the fruit's soft shoulders and juicy flesh make it a fresh-eating and slicing tomato rather than one suited to canning or long storage. In the Deep South it performs best in the spring crop before peak summer heat interferes with fruit set, so get transplants in as early as the weather allows and mulch well to keep roots cool. As an open-pollinated heirloom, seed saves true from year to year with basic isolation from other tomato varieties.
